Before we start

What your business needs in place.

What blocks these is access and ownership, not difficulty.

Admin access to every tool involved

Not a colleague's login — proper admin, and API keys where they exist. Half the delay on an integration is waiting for someone to grant access nobody wants to be responsible for.

The process written down, including the exceptions

Especially the exceptions. The happy path is the easy part; what happens when the customer does not reply, or the stock is wrong, is where the design actually lives.

A person who owns the exceptions

Automation does not remove judgement, it concentrates it. Someone must own the cases the machine hands back, or those cases quietly become a backlog nobody is looking at.

A WhatsApp Business sender, if messaging is involved

An approved sender and template through a provider — not a phone in someone's drawer. Approval takes days and it can be started before anything else.

An honest volume number

Orders or cases per day, and how long each takes now. This is what the price is judged against, and it is what tells us whether the automation is worth building at all.

Terms

How the money and the risk are split.

No retainer to start a conversation, and no invoice for work that never got delivered.

Half to start, half on delivery

The number holds unless you change the scope. If I misjudged it, that is mine.

From the day I have everything on the list, not from the day you pay.

Then hourly, quoted before anything starts. No surprise invoices.

What you send

The handover, in one list.

Send it in one go and the clock starts.

  • The process as it runs today, step by step
  • Admin access and API keys for the tools involved
  • Volume: how many per day, and how long each takes
  • Who handles the exceptions, and how they want them
  • Message templates or wording you already use
  • Any compliance rule the flow must not break

How it runs

Six steps, and you see each one.

  1. 01

    Map

    Walk the process with whoever runs it, including what happens when it goes wrong.

  2. 02

    Cost it

    Hours per week today against the build price. If it does not pay back inside a year, I say so before we start.

  3. 03

    Build

    The flow, the integrations and the exception routing, in a test environment against real data.

  4. 04

    Shadow run

    It runs alongside the manual process for a week. Nothing is switched off until the numbers match.

  5. 05

    Switch over

    Manual step retired, monitoring on, and the team trained on the exception queue.

  6. 06

    Measure

    Back to the number from step two. Either it saved what we said, or we find out why.

Scope

What this is not, and who it is not for.

These are quoted separately, so the price above stays a price.

  • Subscriptions to the tools being connected
  • WhatsApp or SMS message fees
  • Rewriting the systems being integrated
  • Staffing the exception queue
  • Data cleaning of historical records
  • Process consulting beyond what the build requires

Right fit, wrong fit

Saves a call that would end in no.

A good fit

  • Someone retypes the same data into two systems
  • COD returns are eating the margin
  • A process depends on one person remembering
  • You want it measured, not just automated
  • You already pay for tools that do not talk to each other

Not a fit

  • The process changes every week and nobody can describe it
  • Nobody will own the exception queue
  • The volume is too low to pay back — I will tell you if it is
  • You want AI in it regardless of whether it helps

After launch

Once it is running.

Automation fails silently — a token expires, an API changes a field, a carrier renames a status. Nobody notices for a fortnight, and then it is a fortnight of orders. The Care plan is monitoring plus somebody who knows the flow.

Questions

The ones people actually ask.

How do you know it will pay back?

We count first. Hours per week times the loaded cost of the person doing them, against the build price. If it does not clear inside a year I will say so, and that has happened more than once.

Will it replace people?

Usually it replaces the worst part of someone's day, not the person. Where headcount is genuinely the point, say so up front — it changes what is worth building and what needs to be watertight.

What happens when it breaks?

It alerts, it retries, and anything it cannot resolve goes to a person with the context attached. The design assumption is that it will fail sometimes, because it will.

Do we have to change tools?

No. The default is connecting what you already pay for. If a tool genuinely cannot do it, I will show you why rather than assert it.

Can our team change it later?

The simple parts — message wording, timings, thresholds — yes, and the handover covers exactly that. Structural changes are a conversation, and usually a small one.
